deb http://http.us.debian.org/debian   stable         main contrib non-
free
deb http://security.debian.org         lenny/updates  main contrib non-
free
deb http://security.debian.org         stable/updates main contrib non-
free

$SUDO $APT update

$SUDO $APT -y install pkg-config

$LDCONFIG

>
> Tried to follow this. Used seq_along(x) ('x' is an object I created
> earlier) instead of map.values and got the error that object 'x'
> cannot be found(while running rhex). Why is this?

Objects you create in the R environment won't be passed to the map expression.
when inout[1] is 'lapply', map.values contains integers 1 ... N where
N is specified in rhmr.

You can manually use rhwrite to write your list to disk and then
inout=c("seq",'seq") and the rhwite output
can be your input.

>
> Next I tried to solve this by creating 'x' inside the map expression
> itself by:
>
> x = rhread(blah blah blah)
>
> and got the error that 'function rhread cannot be found' once again

You cannot use rhread inside the map expression. The documentation
says what functions are available to the rhipe user
in the map and reduce expression:  rhcollect, rhstatus and rhcounter.

> during rhex !!!!!!!!!!

No need to get excited.

> Now tell me when rhcollect() can be found inside the map expression y
> the hell can rhread() not be found?????

Relax. Reserve your frustration. Why the hell
1. Do  book publishers have greedy control over ebooks?
2. Google becoming  the gateway to the worlds books?
3. prop 8 was voted yes in California?
4. can the US not provide health care to all?
and many more ...

rhread is designed to read from the HDFS. In the mapreduce code, I
have no intention of allowing the user reading from the HDFS.
You can share datasets using the shared parameter which copies the
HDFS backed data to the local side.

> length(seq_along(x)),  but if i do my 'x=rhread(blah blah blah)' (if
> that can be done) inside the map expression, how can i access that
> value in my rhmr for N?
>

Because it's not available. Use inout=c("seq","seq"), write your list
objectusing rhwrite and use that folder
as an ifolder.

(Quick digression) if you're using data frames in RHIPE, try and set

the data frame using rhwrite, and the rhread it again. You get (what
you saw):

[1] 7 5 7

Each column is key-value pair. The key is the column name, the value
is the column.

You want to convert this into {Cuboid, (5,6,7) }, {Cube, (5,5,5)}.

1. Now if your data frame (8GB) is massive, you're not going to read

Pyramid      4       4      7

>  list(k = t[[1]][[r]], v = list(L= t [[2]][[r]], B=t[[3]][[r]],
> H=t[[4]][[r]]))

You could do

rows.of.lines <- strsplit(unlist(map.values)," ")
shape <- unlist(lapply(rows.lines,"[[",1))
lengths <- as.numeric(unlist(lapply(rows.lines,"[[",2))
breadth <- as.numeric(unlist(lapply(rows.lines,"[[",3))
height <- as.numeric(unlist(lapply(rows.lines,"[[",3))

for(i in seq_along(rows.of.lines))
  rhcollect(shape[[i]], c(lengths[[i]],breadth[[i]], height[[i]]))

Your data set is now key-value of the shape you desire.

if that is the case, then write it to disk, (stripping of row.names
and column.names), save it to the HDFS
